instruction: none: started by the service for timer
headline: Started by this line's timer to stop the same-instant loops where a sphere joins a moving stack and is undone at once (seed 1 at f* 0.3 near 5.9205, f* 0.4 at 5.2816). They turned out to have one cause: at the instant of the join another contact of the stack is still sliding with a tiny slip, under which the new contact would pull; a moment later it sticks and the new contact would push. Keeping the detached sphere inside the stack until it really touches again (D0103) gets the f* 0.4 layer through the step to 5.29; seed 1's step with that change had not finished after 19.5 minutes, so it is untested.

experiments.question: Why is the touch of a sphere whose join was just undone reported again at the same instant?
experiments.what_was_done: Saved the layer at the loop instant so it replays in seconds, then compared the search's decision, the contact-force matrix and the stack's motion just after the instant.
experiments.result: The search was right to report it: the pair really closes, by about 1e-13 within a millionth of a time unit. The force matrix is well conditioned (condition number 30). The cause is a disagreement about modes: the joined stack starts with all contacts sliding, so the new contact needs a pull of 0.41 and is dropped; the stack left behind has a plate contact sliding at a slip of about 1e-11 that sticks within a billionth of a time unit, after which the free sphere closes again. A second bug was found: a stack hit at the very instant its stored path starts used the contact modes from the end of that path.
experiments.takeaway: The loop is about choosing contact modes at the start instant, not about round-off approaches as the last run thought.

experiments.question: Does keeping drifted rolling contacts rolling at a new stack's start (D0101, with the start-instant modes fixed) stop the loops?
experiments.what_was_done: Replayed both loops from saved states.
experiments.result: No. In seed 1 the rule acted (18 contacts kept rolling) and the loop moved later by 3e-7 time units, same spheres. In the f* 0.4 layer it did not act, because the plate contact there really was sliding at the start, and the loop stayed at the same instant.
experiments.takeaway: Needed for consistency, but not the fix.

experiments.question: Does reporting a touch where the gap actually crosses the search floor (D0102), rather than where the pair first comes within round-off, stop the loops?
experiments.what_was_done: Replayed both loops from saved states.
experiments.result: No. It acted in both, and both loop at new instants: f* 0.4 at 5.2815952, seed 1 at 5.9205062, which is earlier than with D0101 alone. In both, a contact elsewhere in the stack slides with a small slip (1.5e-7 and 3.4e-5); with it sliding the new contact would pull (push -0.41 and -0.079), with it rolling it would push (+0.43 and +0.37). The sphere handed back is already past the search floor, so it touches again at once.
experiments.takeaway: Shows the mechanism directly in both layers: handing the sphere back at the start instant is what makes the loop.

experiments.question: Does keeping a sphere detached by a pulling contact at a stack's start inside the stack, with no contact, until its gap really closes (D0103), get both layers past their loops?
experiments.what_was_done: Replayed f* 0.4 from the saved state at 5.2816 to 5.29, and seed 1 from 5.92 to 5.93.
experiments.result: f* 0.4 completes the step to 5.29 in 240 seconds of CPU, with 31 spheres kept this way, 27 of them joined later where they really touched, at most 8 handler calls at one instant, no sphere handed back overlapping, and no touch gaining more than 1.5e-15 of energy. Seed 1's step was still running after 19.5 minutes with no output when the run had to end; earlier versions took 1.5 to 5 minutes for it.
experiments.takeaway: The f* 0.4 layer passes the point where it had been stuck since November 27. Whether seed 1 passes, or the change makes it crawl, is not known yet.

proposed_directions.direction: Rerun seed 1's step 5.92 to 5.93 with the new rule, a CPU cap, and a log written at every handler call, then run the f* 0.4 and seed 2 layers on toward the end of cycle 0.
proposed_directions.rationale: The new rule is the first to get a layer past its loop; seed 1 either passes or shows a new cost problem, and the trace script only writes at its end, which hid which one this run.

proposed_directions.direction: Detect singular contact-force matrices by their condition number and use the least-squares forces for them.
proposed_directions.rationale: E0117 found 38 of 300 random rolling stacks singular without numpy noticing; real stacks have not been checked, and wrong forces there could produce pulls like the ones traced this run.

proposed_directions.direction: Time the cheaper force solve in a whole layer and join all spheres touching at one instant in one step.
proposed_directions.rationale: Stack cost decides whether the method can run the long-contact test at all; the f* 0.4 step to 5.29 still took 240 seconds for 0.008 time units.

unfinished_runs.reason: The seed 1 trace (5.92 to 5.93) was still running at 05:49Z after 20 minutes with no output; the process is not visible from later shell calls and does not survive the run, so it was not collected. If runs/E0122/trace_s1.json appears, the next run records the folder again and reads it.
